title: -'s (your sister's name) and of ... (the name of the book)
subtitle: Tom's computer / the name of the book
summary: Use -'s for people, animals and time words, and of ... for things and ideas.

lesson.heading: -'s for people and animals
lesson.text: We use -'s (apostrophe + s) mostly for people or animals. You can use -'s without a noun after it. But we do not use -'s after a long group of words.

examples.text: What's **your sister's name**? What's **Tom's sister's name**?
Be careful. Don't step on **the cat's tail**.
This isn't my book. It's **my sister's**.
**my friend's mother** but **the mother of the man we met yesterday**
examples.wrong: the man we met yesterday's mother

lesson.note: We also say a woman's hat (= a hat for a woman), a boy's name (= a name for a boy), a bird's egg (= an egg laid by a bird).

lesson.heading: Singular or plural noun?
rows: my sister's room (= her room - one sister); Mr Carter's house
my sisters' room (= their room - two or more sisters); the Carters' house
the men's changing room; a children's book (= a book for children)
Jack and Karen's children; Mr and Mrs Carter's house

lesson.heading: of ... for things
lesson.text: For things and ideas we normally use of, not -'s. We also say the beginning/end/middle of ..., the top/bottom of ..., the front/back/side of ...

examples.text: **the name of the book**, **the owner of the restaurant**
**the top of the hill**, **the back of the car**

lesson.heading: Organisations and places: both are possible
lesson.text: For an organisation (= a group of people) you can usually use -'s or of ... We also use -'s for places.

examples.text: **the government's decision** or **the decision of the government**
**the company's success** or **the success of the company**
**the city's streets**, **the world's population**, **Italy's prime minister**

lesson.heading: -'s with time words
lesson.text: We use -'s with time words such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, this evening, next week and Monday. We also use -'s (or -s' with plural words) with periods of time.

examples.text: I've got **a week's holiday** starting on Monday.
I live near the station - it's only **ten minutes' walk**.

lesson.text: People and animals: -'s (Tom's car). Things: of (the door of the car). Time: -'s again (tomorrow's meeting, two hours' drive).

exercises.prompt: Which is the natural way to ask this? How old are ___?
exercises.explanation: For people we use -'s: Chris's children.
A person, so -'s: your friend's umbrella.

exercises.statement: Write your name at the top of the page.
exercises.explanation: Correct. For things we use of: the top of the page (not the page's top).
A singular name takes -'s, even when it ends in -s: James's daughter.

exercises.statement: The garden of our neighbours is very small.
exercises.explanation: Our neighbours' garden is very small. For people we use -'s; a plural ending in -s takes -s'.
children is a plural that does not end in -s, so we add -'s: Children's clothes.
Two parents = a plural ending in -s, so the apostrophe goes after the s: parents'.

exercises.prompt: Would you use -'s or of ... to join these? The noun in brackets is the owner or the thing it belongs to.
Put the words in order. Begin with the time expression.
exercises.answer: Last week's storm caused a lot of damage.
exercises.explanation: Time words take -'s: last week's storm.
We use -'s for places: Switzerland's largest city.

exercises.prompt: If I leave my house at 8.40 and walk to the centre, I get there at 9 o'clock. So it's ___ from my house to the centre.
exercises.explanation: A period of time takes -s' (plural): twenty minutes' walk.

exercises.prompt: I'm going on holiday on the 12th. I have to be back at work on the 26th. So I've got ___.
exercises.explanation: Periods of time: two weeks' holiday (plural -s') or a fortnight's holiday (singular -'s).
